 - Meteorological Overview:

A moist southwesterly flow aloft continues to overrun a cooler 
and nearly saturated air mass at the surface. The Pacific NW 
trough responsible for the moist southwesterly flow ejects 
eastward towards the Northern Rockies and sends waves of more 
widespread precipitation through the forecast area today through 
Monday morning. This system will be undergoing weakening and 
shearing as it approaches and its colder air aloft is not 
scheduled to arrive until tonight into Monday morning. So snow 
levels will be over 7000 ft for most locations, generally yielding
liquid precipitation at and below pass level. The one exception 
to this will be along the Continental Divide where spotty light 
snow will fall before tonight.

H700 temperatures finally fall to around -5C late night into 
early Monday and this will bring more efficient accumulating snow,
heaviest over the Madison/Gallatin ranges above 6000 ft. There 
will be a brief period with snow levels falling to the 
valley/plains floors Monday morning, although it does not appear 
that this will be long enough to support widespread accumulating 
snow impacts. Northwesterly winds may also get gusty later 
tonight, though gusts look to stay below 40 mph and the strongest 
winds should quickly move east of the forecast area Monday 
morning. Ensembles continue to favor ridging aloft to bring milder
and drier conditions for much of the upcoming workweek; however, 
a weak system may move through around Wednesday and bring a few 
isolated showers to the southwest and along the Continental 
Divide. - RCG

As rain tapers off over Sunday night and Monday morning, lighter 
winds and higher overnight humidity levels will allow for areas of
fog to potentially develop within central MT, north-central MT, 
and the southwest valleys. Due to limited winds during the rest of
the Monday, there is the possibility that these areas of fog 
remain socked in as they have the past few days, resulting in 
daytime highs falling 5-10 degrees below what was expected in 
those areas.

Looking towards the rest of the week, an upper-level ridge begins
to establish over the region beginning Monday evening. Accompanying
this ridge will be mild and dry weather. Although the upper- 
level ridge is expected to weaken beginning Tuesday night, dry 
and mild conditions are currently expected to remain in place 
through at least Thursday afternoon. Although far out, a change in
the weather is anticipated on Friday due to an upper-level trough
beginning to move into the area, along with windier conditions. 
-ESH


 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

...Light mountain snow and lower elevation rain and snow Sunday 
through Monday morning...

The main trough swings through today through early Monday and 
brings a wave of widespread precipitation to much of the forecast 
area. Aside from some light snow along the Continental Divide and 
perhaps some spotty freezing drizzle over the plains west of I15, 
most of the precipitation will be falling in the form of rain 
until the colder air aloft moves in tonight. The overall pattern 
and NBM probabilities continue to favor elevations over 6000 ft in
the Madison and Gallatin ranges for the best chance (60 to 80%) 
of snowfall amounts in excess of 3 inches. Lighter snows, 
generally up to a couple inches, look to fall along the 
Continental Divide and the central island ranges. The colder air 
is still not looking to be optimally aligned with the moisture for
lower elevation snows, even in the Gallatin Valley where 
probabilities for 2 inches of snow fell from around 30% to around 
10%. Decided to hold off on issuing any winter advisories with 
this forecast package given the brief window of opportunity for 
accumulating snow at and below pass level and H700 temperatures 
trending upward ever so slightly. - RCG

...Fog during the upcoming week...

The main time period of concern will be Sunday night into Monday
morning as precip moves through the region and tapers off. Lighter
winds, along with residual moisture, will provide favorable
conditions for fog development. The main impact associated with
this would be a reduction in visibility and the potential for
freezing fog due to overnight lows expected to be near or below
freezing. If areas of denser fog develop, there is the potential
for that fog to remain socked in and keep daytime high
temperatures 5-10 degrees cooler than expected. Through the rest 
of the upcoming work week, pockets of fog may develop overnight, 
although these would likely be patchy and limited to areas near 
bodies of water and valleys. -ESH
